gap: No result ChatGPT got turns the screens' advertised diagonals into the picture you actually get for a 16:9 movie. By Elite Screens' own conversion, a square-format Tripod screen sold as 113 inches shows a 92-inch 16:9 picture (80 × 45 in). That is smaller than the 105-inch Yard Master 2, whose 16:9 surface is about 91.5 × 51.5 in, roughly 24% less picture area.
standout_why: I opened projectorverdict.com/best/best-tripod-projector-screen (2026-10-30). It lists the Elite Tripod as '100"–120"', '16:9 or 4:3' and '1.1 gain', but gives no viewable dimensions anywhere. Its only note on format is 'Mixing the two wastes real screen area as black bars', with no number. ChatGPT's own answer puts the Tripod card ($142) next to the Yard Master 2 (105") and the 100" VEVOR as if their sizes compare directly. I could not open the cited Wirecutter page (nytimes blocked the fetch and the proxy returned 403) or Esquire (fetch blocked), so I cannot rule out that they cover this. That is why I scored 2 and not 3.
decides: This backs the Yard Master 2 as the movie pick. Elite's 1:1 and 4:3 Tripod sizes are measured across a square or 4:3 surface, so a 16:9 movie fills about 80 × 45 in of a '100"' 4:3 or '113"' 1:1 Tripod, which works out to 92 inches. The Yard Master 2's 1.3-gain CineWhite UHD-B is also brighter than the Tripod's 1.1-gain MaxWhite 2. Anyone buying a Tripod for movies should choose a 16:9 Tripod model (60"–120"), not the 1:1 or 4:3 ones that ChatGPT's 'Best for presentations' card covers. The Aurzen 120" (1.1 gain, 16:9, $24.99) is the low-cost way to get a picture bigger than 100 inches, but stock pages don't say whether it includes a stand.
